903--- Note to developers:
904---     Per Github discussion: Lean's convention is to prefer
905---     the declaration header style
906---     (`mul_zero  (n : Nat) : n * zero = zero`) over universal
907---     quantification style
908---     (`mul_zero : ∀ (n : Nat), n * zero = zero`). We probably
909---     still want to teach the universal quantification style
910---     at first, but should switch over to declaration header
911---     style quickly since that is the idiomatic Lean way to do

3+-- # Postscript
4+
5+-- Note to developers:
6+--     The FULL version could use some real text
7+
8+-- Congratulations: We've made it to the end of *Logical
9+-- Foundations*!
10+
11+-- ## Looking Back
12+
13+-- We've covered quite a bit of ground so far. Here's a quick
14+-- review...
15+
16+-- - *Functional programming*:
17+
18+--   - "declarative" programming style (recursion over immutable
19+--     data structures, rather than looping over mutable arrays or
20+--     pointer structures)
21+
22+--   - higher-order functions
23+
24+--   - polymorphism
25+
26+-- - *Logic*, the mathematical basis for software engineering:
27+
28+-- logic                        calculus
29+-- --------------------   ~   ----------------------------
30+-- software engineering       mechanical/civil engineering
31+
32+-- - inductively defined sets and relations
33+-- - inductive proofs
34+-- - proof objects
35+
36+-- - *Lean*, an industrial-strength proof assistant
37+-- - functional core language
38+-- - core tactics
39+-- - automation
40+
41+-- ## Looking Forward
42+
43+-- OLD: If what you've seen so far has whetted your interest,
44+-- you have several choices for further reading in later
45+-- volumes of the *Software Foundations* series. Some of these
46+-- are intended to be accessible to readers immediately after
47+-- finishing *Logical Foundations*; others require a few
48+-- chapters from Volume 2, *Programming Language Foundations*.
49+-- The Preface chapter in each volume gives details about
50+-- prerequisites.
51+
52+-- FINISH: As of August 2026, there are two more volumes
53+-- written in Lean.
54+
55+-- *Hoare Logic*: This short volume describes one of the
56+-- primary methods for reasoning about *imperative* programs-
57+-- programs with state and mutation, like C++, Java, C, and
58+-- Assembly- in a pure logic like Lean's. This method, called
59+-- *Hoare Logic*, is embeddable into Lean's type system and is
60+-- a powerful tool for determining the correct behavior of
61+-- imperative code. Since most of the code in the wild today is
62+-- imperative, this technique is both well-established and
63+-- popular among industry professionals who analyze and fortify
64+-- the correctness of systems.
65+
66+-- *Type Systems*: Another tool for reasoning about the
67+-- correctness of a program is a *type system*. You have
68+-- interacted thoroughly with Lean's rich type system, which is
69+-- one of the most complex in a modern programming language.
70+-- Most languages have type systems that are far less complex,
71+-- but which still provide incredibly useful guardrails against
72+-- ill-behaved programs. In this volume you will explore how to
73+-- read, analyze, and design type systems in a proof assistant.
74+
75+-- Note to developers (before next release):
76+--     `Might be worth explicitly advertising each volume, like
77+--     this?  Some danger of redunancy tho...
78+--
79+--             - _Programming Language Foundations_ (volume 2, by a set of
80+--               authors similar to this book's) covers material that
81+--               might be found in a graduate course on the theory of
82+--               programming languages, including Hoare logic, operational
83+--               semantics, and type systems.
84+--
85+--             - _Verified Functional Algorithms_ (volume 3, by Andrew
86+--               Appel) builds on the themes of functional programming and
87+--               program verification in Rocq, addressing a range of topics
88+--               that might be found in a standard data structures course,
89+--               with an eye to formal verification.`
90+
91+-- ## Resources
92+
93+-- Here are some other good places to learn more...
94+
95+-- - This book includes some optional chapters covering topics
96+--   that you may find useful. Take a look at the #<a
97+--   href="toc.html">#table of contents#</a># and the #<a
98+--   href="deps.html">#chapter dependency diagram#</a># to find
99+--   them.
100+
101+-- - For questions about Rocq, the `#coq` area of Stack Overflow
102+--   (<https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/coq>) is an
103+--   excellent community resource.
104+
105+-- - Here are some great books on functional programming
106+
107+--   - Learn You a Haskell for Great Good, by Miran Lipovaca
108+--     Lipovaca 2011.
109+
110+--   - Real World Haskell, by Bryan O'Sullivan, John Goerzen, and
111+--     Don Stewart O'Sullivan 2008
112+
113+--   - ...and many other excellent books on Haskell, OCaml, Scheme,
114+--     Racket, Scala, F sharp, etc., etc.
115+
116+-- - And some further resources for Rocq:
117+
118+--   - Certified Programming with Dependent Types, by Adam Chlipala
119+--     Chlipala 2013.
120+
121+--   - Interactive Theorem Proving and Program Development:
122+--     Coq'Art: The Calculus of Inductive Constructions, by Yves
123+--     Bertot and Pierre Casteran Bertot 2004.
124+
125+-- - If you're interested in real-world applications of formal
126+--   verification to critical software, see the Postscript
127+--   chapter of *Programming Language Foundations*.
128+
129+-- - For applications of Rocq in building verified systems, the
130+--   lectures and course materials for the 2017 DeepSpec Summer
131+--   School are a great resource.
132+--   <https://deepspec.org/event/dsss17/index.html>

33 -- # Preface
44 
5--- Testing .
6-
5+-- ## Welcome
6+
7+-- This is the entry point to a series of electronic textbooks
8+-- on various aspects of *Software Foundations*, the
9+-- mathematical underpinnings of reliable software. Topics in
10+-- the series include basic concepts of logic, functional
11+-- programming, computer-assisted theorem proving, operational
12+-- semantics, logics and techniques for reasoning about
13+-- programs, static type systems, property-based random
14+-- testing, and verification of practical C code. The
15+-- exposition is intended for a broad range of readers, from
16+-- advanced undergraduates to PhD students and researchers. No
17+-- specific background in logic or programming languages is
18+-- assumed, though a degree of mathematical maturity will be
19+-- helpful.
20+
21+-- The principal novelty of the series is that it is one
22+-- hundred percent formalized and machine-checked: each text is
23+-- literally a script for Lean. The books are intended to be
24+-- read alongside (or inside) an interactive session with Lean.
25+-- All the details in the text are fully formalized in Lean,
26+-- and almost all of the exercises are designed to be worked
27+-- using Lean.
28+
29+-- This book, *Logical Foundations in Lean*, lays groundwork
30+-- for the others, introducing the reader to the basic ideas of
31+-- functional programming, formal logic, and Lean itself.
32+
33+-- ## Overview
34+
35+-- Building reliable software is hard -- really hard. The scale
36+-- and complexity of modern systems, the number of people
37+-- involved, and the range of demands placed on them make it
38+-- challenging to build software that is even more-or-less
39+-- correct, much less 100% correct. At the same time, the
40+-- increasing degree to which information processing is woven
41+-- into every aspect of society greatly amplifies the cost of
42+-- bugs and insecurities.
43+
44+-- Computer scientists and software engineers have responded to
45+-- these challenges with a host of techniques for improving
46+-- software reliability, ranging from recommendations about
47+-- managing software projects teams (e.g., extreme programming)
48+-- to design philosophies for libraries (e.g.,
49+-- model-view-controller, publish-subscribe, etc.) and whole
50+-- programming languages (e.g., object-oriented programming,
51+-- functional programming, ...) to mathematical techniques for
52+-- specifying and reasoning about properties of software and
53+-- tools for helping validate these properties. The *Software
54+-- Foundations* books are focused on this last set of tools.
55+
56+-- The present volume weaves together three conceptual threads:
57+
58+-- - basic tools from *logic* for making and justifying precise
59+--   claims about programs;
60+
61+-- - the use of *provers* (or *proof assistants*) to construct
62+--   rigorous logical arguments;
63+
64+-- - *functional programming*, both as a programming method that
65+--   simplifies reasoning about programs and as a bridge between
66+--   programming and logic.
67+
68+-- ### Logic
69+
70+-- Logic is the field of study whose subject matter is *proofs*
71+-- -- unassailable arguments for the truth of particular
72+-- propositions. Volumes have been written about the central
73+-- role of logic in computer science. Manna and Waldinger
74+-- called it "the calculus of computer science," while Halpern
75+-- et al.'s paper *On the Unusual Effectiveness of Logic in
76+-- Computer Science* catalogs scores of ways in which logic
77+-- offers critical tools and insights. Indeed, they observe
78+-- that, "As a matter of fact, logic has turned out to be
79+-- significantly more effective in computer science than it has
80+-- been in mathematics. This is quite remarkable, especially
81+-- since much of the impetus for the development of logic
82+-- during the past one hundred years came from mathematics."
83+
84+-- In particular, the fundamental tools of *inductive proof*
85+-- are ubiquitous across computer science. You have surely seen
86+-- them before, perhaps in a course on discrete math or
87+-- analysis of algorithms, but in this book we will examine
88+-- them more deeply than you have probably done so far.
89+
90+-- ### Proof Assistants
91+
92+-- The flow of ideas between logic and computer science over
93+-- the years has run in both directions, with CS also making
94+-- contributions to logic. One of these has been the
95+-- development of software tools for helping construct and
96+-- validate proofs of logical statements. These tools fall into
97+-- two broad categories:
98+
99+-- - *Automated theorem provers* provide "push-button" operation:
100+--   you give them a proposition and they return either *true* or
101+--   *false* (or, sometimes, *don't know: ran out of time*).
102+--   Although their reasoning capabilities are limited, they have
103+--   matured tremendously in recent decades and are used now in a
104+--   multitude of settings. Examples of such tools include SAT
105+--   solvers, SMT solvers, and model checkers.
106+
107+-- - *Proof assistants* — or just *provers* — are hybrid tools
108+--   that automate the more routine aspects of creating proofs
109+--   while depending on human guidance for more difficult
110+--   aspects. Widely used proof assistants include Isabelle,
111+--   Agda, Twelf, ACL2, PVS, F*, HOL4, Rocq, and Lean, among many
112+--   others.
113+
114+-- This course is based around Lean, a proof assistant that has
115+-- been under development since 2013 and has attracted a large
116+-- and active community of users in both research and at
117+-- companies like DeepMind, OpenAI, Anthropic, MSR, and AWS.
118+
119+-- Lean provides a rich environment for interactive development
120+-- of machine-checked formal reasoning. The kernel of the Lean
121+-- system is a simple proof-checker, which guarantees that only
122+-- correct deduction steps are ever performed. On top of this
123+-- kernel, the Lean environment provides high-level facilities
124+-- for proof development, including a large library of common
125+-- definitions and lemmas, powerful tactics for constructing
126+-- complex proofs semi-automatically, and a highly extensible
127+-- system for defining new proof-automation tactics and
128+-- notations for specific situations.
129+
130+-- Lean and its relatives have become a critical enablers for a
131+-- huge variety of work across computer science and
132+-- mathematics:
133+
134+-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
135+--     Need more examples, including specifically things
136+--     accomplished in Lean.
137+--
138+--     `lean-software-foundations-contributors > Main Achievements of Lean`
139+--     lists some big Lean projects -- some of them should be
140+--     mentioned here. And there are probably things here to
141+--     trim.
142+
143+-- - As a *platform for modeling programming languages*, they
144+--   have become standard tools for researchers who need to
145+--   describe and reason about complex language definitions. They
146+--   have been used, for example, to check the security of the
147+--   JavaCard platform, obtaining the highest level of common
148+--   criteria certification, and for formal specifications of the
149+--   x86 and LLVM instruction sets and programming languages such
150+--   as C.
151+
152+-- - As *environments for developing formally certified software
153+--   and hardware*, they been used, for example, to build
154+--   CompCert, a fully-verified optimizing compiler for C, and
155+--   CertiKOS, a fully verified hypervisor, for proving the
156+--   correctness of subtle algorithms involving floating point
157+--   numbers, and as the basis for CertiCrypt, FCF, and SSProve,
158+--   which are frameworks for proving cryptographic algorithms
159+--   secure. They are also being used to build verified
160+--   implementations of the open-source RISC-V processor
161+--   architecture.
162+
163+-- - As *proof assistants for mathematics*, they have been used
164+--   to validate and help develop a number of important results.
165+--   For example, the ability to include complex computations
166+--   inside proofs made it possible to develop the first formally
167+--   verified proof of the 4-color theorem. This proof had
168+--   previously been controversial among mathematicians because
169+--   it required checking a large number of configurations using
170+--   a program. More recently, an even more massive effort led to
171+--   a formalization of the Feit-Thompson Theorem, the first
172+--   major step in the classification of finite simple groups.
173+
174+-- ### Functional Programming
175+
176+-- *Functional programming* refers both to a collection of
177+-- idioms that can be used in almost any programming language
178+-- and to a family of languages designed to foreground these
179+-- idioms, including Haskell, OCaml, Standard ML, F##, Scala,
180+-- Scheme, Racket, Common Lisp, Clojure, Erlang, F*, and Lean
181+-- itself.
182+
183+-- Functional programming has been developed over many decades
184+-- — indeed, its roots go back to Church's lambda-calculus from
185+-- the 1930s, well *before* the first electronic computers! But
186+-- since the early '90s it has enjoyed a surge of interest
187+-- among both software engineers and language designers.
188+
189+-- The most basic tenet of functional programming is that,
190+-- whenever possible, computation should be *pure*, in the
191+-- sense that the only effect of execution should be to produce
192+-- a result: it should be free from *side effects* such as I/O,
193+-- assignments to mutable variables, redirecting pointers, etc.
194+-- For example, whereas an *imperative* sorting function might
195+-- take a list of numbers and rearrange its pointers to put the
196+-- list in order, a pure sorting function would take the
197+-- original list and return a fresh list containing the same
198+-- numbers in sorted order.
199+
200+-- A significant benefit of this style of programming is that
201+-- it makes programs easier to understand and reason about. If
202+-- every operation on a data structure yields a new data
203+-- structure, leaving the old one intact, then there is no need
204+-- to worry about how that structure is being shared and
205+-- whether a change by one part of the program might break an
206+-- invariant relied on by another part of the program. These
207+-- considerations are particularly critical in concurrent
208+-- systems, where every piece of mutable state shared between
209+-- threads is a potential source of pernicious bugs.
210+
211+-- Another reason for the popularity of functional programming
212+-- is related to the first: functional programs are often much
213+-- easier to parallelize and physically distribute than their
214+-- imperative counterparts. If running a computation has no
215+-- effect other than producing a result, then it does not
216+-- matter *where* it is run. Similarly, if a data structure is
217+-- never modified destructively, it can be copied freely,
218+-- across cores or across the network. Indeed, the "Map-Reduce"
219+-- idiom, which lies at the heart of massively distributed
220+-- query processors like Hadoop and is used by Google to index
221+-- the entire web, is a classic example of functional
222+-- programming.
223+
224+-- For purposes of these books, functional programming has yet
225+-- another significant attraction: it serves as a bridge
226+-- between logic and computer science. Indeed, Lean itself can
227+-- be viewed as a combination of a small but extremely
228+-- expressive functional programming language and a set of
229+-- tools for stating and proving logical assertions. Moreover,
230+-- when we come to look more closely, we find that these two
231+-- sides of Lean are actually aspects of the very same
232+-- underlying machinery -- i.e., *proofs are programs*.
233+
234+-- Note to developers (Benjamin Pierce @bcpierce00):
235+--     Is this an accurate description of Lean?
236+
237+-- ### Further Reading
238+
239+-- This text is intended to be self contained, but readers
240+-- looking for a deeper treatment of particular topics will
241+-- find some suggestions for further reading in the Postscript
242+-- chapter.
243+
244+-- ## Practicalities
245+
246+-- ### System Requirements
247+
248+-- Lean runs on Windows, Linux, and MacOS. The files in this
249+-- book have been tested with Lean version `4.32.0`.
250+
251+-- ### Installation
252+
253+-- The Visual Studio Code IDE is the recommended platform for
254+-- using Lean.
255+
256+-- - Install VS Code if needed
257+
258+-- - From the Extensions tab of VS Code, install the Lean 4
259+--   extension
260+
261+-- - Clone the [SF-in-Lean](https://github.com/plclub/sf-in-lean)
262+--   git repo and open it in VS Code
263+
264+-- - The first time you open a Lean file, the extension will
265+--   offer to install Lean itself; accept, and it will fetch the
266+--   version this book needs
267+
268+-- - Wait for Lean to build the project (it takes a few minutes)
269+
270+-- Note to developers (Claude @AI assistant, before next release):
271+--     These steps send the reader to the **sources** repo, but
272+--     the files a reader is meant to work in are the ones the
273+--     build generates: `make lf-student` writes a standalone
274+--     Lake project (its own `lakefile.toml` and
275+--     `lean-toolchain`) to `_out/lf/student/lean`, and that is
276+--     where the exercises with `sorry`s live. The `LF/*.lean`
277+--     files in the repo are Verso documents — prose plus code
278+--     blocks — and building the repo builds Verso and all
279+--     three volumes, which is a good deal more than "a few
280+--     minutes".
281+--
282+--     There is also a chicken-and-egg problem in the ordering:
283+--     running `make` at all needs `elan`/`lake` already
284+--     installed, but the step above gets Lean via the VS Code
285+--     extension, which only offers it once a Lean project is
286+--     open.
287+--
288+--     Both go away once there is a released archive of the
289+--     student `.lean` files: the steps become "download and
290+--     unpack, open the folder in VS Code, accept the install
291+--     prompt". Until that exists, this section should probably
292+--     say plainly that readers get the files from their
293+--     instructor or by following `ALPHATESTERS.md`.
294+
295+-- ### Exercises
296+
297+-- Each chapter includes numerous exercises. Each is marked
298+-- with a "star rating," which can be interpreted as follows:
299+
300+-- - One star: easy exercises that underscore points in the text
301+--   and that, for most readers, should take only a minute or
302+--   two. Get in the habit of working these as you reach them.
303+
304+-- - Two stars: straightforward exercises (five or ten minutes).
305+
306+-- - Three stars: exercises requiring a bit of thought (ten
307+--   minutes to half an hour).
308+
309+-- - Four and five stars: more difficult exercises (half an hour
310+--   and up).
311+
312+-- Those using SF in a classroom setting should note that the
313+-- autograder assigns extra points to harder exercises:
314+
315+-- 1 star  = 1 point
316+-- 2 stars = 2 points
317+-- 3 stars = 3 points
318+-- 4 stars = 6 points
319+-- 5 stars = 10 points
320+
321+-- Some exercises are marked "advanced," and some are marked
322+-- "optional." Doing just the non-optional, non-advanced
323+-- exercises should provide good coverage of the core material.
324+-- Optional exercises provide a bit of extra practice with key
325+-- concepts and introduce secondary themes that may be of
326+-- interest to some readers. Advanced exercises offer an extra
327+-- challenge and a deeper cut at the ideas.
328+
329+-- ### Citation Format
330+
331+-- If you want to refer to this volume in your own writing,
332+-- please do so as follows:
333+
334+-- @book            {SFL:1,
335+-- author       =   {Mike Hicks and Benjamin C. Pierce and the SF-in-Lean team},
336+-- title        =   "Logical Foundations",
337+-- series       =   "Software Foundations in Lean",
338+-- volume       =   "1",
339+-- year         =   "2026",
340+-- publisher    =   "Electronic textbook",
341+-- note         =   {Version 0.1.0, \URL<https://github.com/plclub/sf-in-lean>}
342+-- }
343+
344+-- ## For Potential Contributors
345+
346+-- If you find things you'd like to help add or improve, your
347+-- contributions are welcome! To get started, clone the
348+-- [SF-in-Lean git repo](https://github.com/plclub/sf-in-lean)
349+-- and have a look at `ALPHATESTERS.md`.
350+
351+-- ## For Instructors
352+
353+-- A large compendium of exams from many offerings of CIS5000
354+-- ("Software Foundations") at the University of Pennsylvania
355+-- can be found at
356+-- <https://www.seas.upenn.edu/~cis5000/current/exams/index.html>.
357+-- Until 2026, the course was offered in Rocq, but the ideas
358+-- behind the problems are still relevant.
359+
360+-- ## Acknowledgements
361+
362+-- See `ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS.md` in the [SF-in-Lean git
363+-- repo](https://github.com/plclub/sf-in-lean).
364+
